generation_meta_data.title: Frontend migration: OpenGraphQL type generation replacement
generation_meta_data.description: Replace OpenGraphQL type generation with alternative solution. Initial attempt blocked by tight coupling with schema introspection. Need to investigate dependency chain and find suitable replacement.

generation_meta_data.message: I need to do some git archaeology to understand how OpenGraphQL got so deeply embedded. Going to trace through the commit history to see the evolution.

Found the smoking gun! Commit from March 2022 (hash: a4f7b81) shows the original auth integration. The file src/auth/validators/GraphQLUserValidator.js directly imports OpenGraphQL schema objects instead of using the API layer.
@bob That explains a lot. I'm seeing similar tight coupling in the build scripts. The Docker images compile OpenGraphQL schemas at build time, not runtime.
@bob @charlie This is worse than I thought. My frontend migration failed because GraphQL types are generated during the backend build process. There's a circular dependency I didn't know about.

@diana Exactly! The build system expects OpenGraphQL schema validation to happen before GraphQL types are generated. But diana's migration approach generates types first, then validates schemas - hence the undefined reference errors.

generation_meta_data.title: Build system analysis: OpenGraphQL circular dependencies
generation_meta_data.description: Analysis reveals circular dependency in build process: OpenGraphQL schema validation must happen before type generation, but migration approaches attempt reverse order. Root cause: build scripts assume OpenGraphQL schema objects exist at compile time.

generation_meta_data.message: Team, we need to understand why the original integration was designed this way. There must have been constraints that led to this tight coupling. Let me dig into the historical context.

Found it! Git blame shows the original coupling was introduced to meet a sub-100ms API response requirement in 2022. The architect decided to share schema objects directly instead of making API calls to avoid the latency overhead.
@alice That makes perfect sense now. The performance requirement forced the tight coupling. We need to redesign with that constraint in mind.

generation_meta_data.title: Historical analysis: Original OpenGraphQL integration constraints
generation_meta_data.description: Investigation reveals original tight coupling was designed to meet sub-100ms API response requirement from 2022. Direct schema object sharing was chosen over API calls to avoid latency overhead. This constraint must be preserved in migration strategy.

generation_meta_data.message: @alice @charlie Based on the historical analysis, I think we need a phased migration approach. First establish the shared schema layer, then migrate each component while preserving performance.
Now that I understand the build order requirements, I can redesign the frontend migration. Need to wait for bob's shared schema layer before proceeding.

generation_meta_data.message: @bob The shared schema approach is working! Build times are actually faster now. The performance constraint led us to a better architecture.
